questions.stem: If E(X) = 5, then E(2X + 3) equals:
questions.explanation: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b = 2 × 5 + 3 = 13. Adding 3 before doubling gives 16, which would be E(2(X + 3)).

questions.stem: If Var(X) = 4, then Var(2X + 3) equals:
questions.explanation: Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X), so Var(2X + 3) = 4 × 4 = 16. Adding a constant shifts every value equally and leaves the spread unchanged; doubling without squaring gives 8.

questions.stem: X and Y are independent with Var(X) = 9 and Var(Y) = 4. Then Var(X − Y) equals:
questions.explanation: For independent variables Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + (−1)²Var(Y) = 9 + 4 = 13. Subtracting the variances gives 5, but subtracting a random quantity adds variability.

questions.stem: A population has standard deviation 12. For samples of size 36, the standard deviation of the sample mean is:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of the sample mean is σ/√n = 12/√36 = 2. Dividing by n instead of √n gives 1/3.

questions.stem: The mean of the distribution of sample means, for random samples of size n from a population with mean μ, is:
questions.explanation: The sample mean is an unbiased estimator: its expected value is the population mean μ for every n. The factor √n affects the standard deviation, not the mean.

questions.stem: For a large sample size n, the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal:
options: only if the population is symmetric
only if n is close to the population size
whatever the shape of the population distribution
only if the population is normal
questions.explanation: For large n the sample mean is approximately normal even for skewed or discrete populations. A normal population makes it exactly normal for every n, but that is not required.

questions.stem: For an approximate 95% confidence interval, the standard normal quantile used is about:
questions.explanation: 95% of the standard normal distribution lies between −1.96 and 1.96. The value 1.645 is for 90% (or a one-tailed 5% test) and 2.576 is for 99%.

questions.stem: In a hypothesis test about a population mean μ, the null hypothesis H₀ is:
options: that μ differs from a stated value
that μ equals a stated value
the claim the researcher hopes to support
that the sample mean equals a stated value
questions.explanation: H₀ states that the population mean has a particular value, such as μ = 500. Hypotheses are about the population parameter, not the sample mean, and the claim the researcher hopes to support is usually H₁.

questions.stem: The p-value of a hypothesis test is the probability, assuming H₀ is true, of:
options: a sample mean exactly equal to the one observed
a sample mean at least as extreme as the one observed
questions.explanation: The p-value is calculated assuming H₀, so it cannot be the probability that H₀ is true. For a continuous distribution any exact value has probability 0, which is why the tail is used.

questions.stem: A test at the 5% level of significance gives a p-value of 0.03. The correct decision is to:
options: reject H₀ in favour of H₁
questions.explanation: The p-value is less than the significance level 0.05, so the result is significant and H₀ is rejected. A test never proves H₀; at most it fails to find evidence against it.

questions.stem: A type I error is:
options: not rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true
rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true
not rejecting H₀ when H₀ is false
rejecting H₀ when H₀ is false
questions.explanation: A type I error rejects a true null hypothesis, and its probability is the significance level. Not rejecting a false H₀ is a type II error; the other two are correct decisions.

questions.stem: A machine fills bottles with a mean of 750 mL. An engineer tests whether the mean has changed. The hypotheses are:
questions.explanation: “Changed” allows either direction, so the alternative is two-tailed. A one-tailed alternative would be used only if the engineer suspected a change in one stated direction.

questions.stem: Apples have masses with mean 150 g and standard deviation 10 g, independently. The total mass of 5 apples has:
options: mean 750 g and standard deviation 10/√5 g
mean 750 g and standard deviation 10√5 g
mean 750 g and standard deviation 50 g
mean 150 g and standard deviation 10√5 g
questions.explanation: For a sum of n independent identically distributed variables the mean is nμ = 750 and the variance is nσ² = 500, so the standard deviation is √500 = 10√5. The value 50 = 5 × 10 treats the total as 5X.

questions.stem: X ~ N(20, 3²) and Y ~ N(30, 4²) are independent. The distribution of X + Y is normal with:
questions.explanation: Means add: 20 + 30 = 50. Variances add for independent variables: 9 + 16 = 25, so the standard deviation is 5. Standard deviations do not add, so 7 is wrong, and 25 is the variance.

questions.stem: E(X) = 4, E(Y) = 1, Var(X) = 2 and Var(Y) = 3, with X and Y independent. Then 3X − 2Y has:
questions.explanation: E(3X − 2Y) = 12 − 2 = 10, and Var(3X − 2Y) = 9 × 2 + 4 × 3 = 30. The coefficients are squared, so the minus sign disappears; subtracting gives 18 − 12 = 6.

questions.stem: A population has μ = 100 and σ = 15. For a random sample of size 25, Pr(sample mean > 106) is about:
questions.explanation: The sample mean has standard deviation 15/√25 = 3, so z = (106 − 100)/3 = 2 and Pr(Z > 2) ≈ 0.023. Using σ = 15 gives z = 0.4 and 0.345, the probability for a single value, not a mean.

questions.stem: Multiplying the sample size by 4 changes the standard deviation of the sample mean by:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is σ/√n, and √(4n) = 2√n, so it halves. To quarter it, the sample size would have to be multiplied by 16.

questions.stem: A random sample of 100 has mean 52, from a population with σ = 10. An approximate 95% confidence interval for μ is:
questions.explanation: The interval is 52 ± 1.96 × 10/√100 = 52 ± 1.96. Dividing by n gives 52 ± 0.196, forgetting √n gives 52 ± 19.6, and 52 ± 1.645 is a 90% interval.

questions.stem: Which statement about 95% confidence intervals for μ is correct?
options: About 95% of the sample’s values lie inside the interval
The sample mean lies inside the interval with probability 0.95
About 95% of intervals made this way, from repeated samples, contain μ
About 95% of the population’s values lie inside the interval
questions.explanation: The 95% describes the method: across many samples, about 95% of the intervals capture μ. The interval estimates the mean, not where individual values lie, and the sample mean is always at the centre of its own interval.

questions.stem: Using the same sample, the confidence level is increased from 95% to 99%. The interval:
options: keeps the same width but moves
questions.explanation: The quantile rises from 1.96 to about 2.576, so the margin of error grows. More confidence of capturing μ costs a less precise interval. The centre is the sample mean, which does not change.

questions.stem: A consumer group suspects that the mean life of a battery is less than the 500 hours claimed. The hypotheses are:
questions.explanation: H₀ is the claim being tested, μ = 500, and the suspicion of a lower mean gives the one-tailed alternative μ < 500. The hypotheses never swap roles: H₀ always contains the equality.

questions.stem: H₀: μ = 100, with σ = 12. A sample of 36 has mean 103. The value of the test statistic z is:
questions.explanation: z = (103 − 100)/(12/√36) = 3/2 = 1.5. Dividing by σ alone gives 0.25, and dividing by σ/n gives 9. The sample mean is above 100, so z is positive.

questions.stem: In a two-tailed test, the test statistic is z = 2.0. The p-value is about:
questions.explanation: Pr(Z ≥ 2) ≈ 0.023, and a two-tailed test counts both tails, so p ≈ 2 × 0.023 = 0.046. The one-tailed value 0.023 is half the p-value.

questions.stem: For H₀: μ = 20 against H₁: μ < 20, the test statistic is z = −1.2. At the 5% level:
options: p ≈ 0.885, so H₀ is not rejected
p ≈ 0.230, so H₀ is not rejected
p ≈ 0.115, so H₀ is not rejected
questions.explanation: The p-value is Pr(Z ≤ −1.2) ≈ 0.115, which is greater than 0.05, so the result is not significant. The value 0.885 is the wrong tail, and 0.230 doubles for a two-tailed test that was not asked for.

questions.stem: A test gives a p-value of 0.30. At the 5% level, the conclusion is that:
options: there is not enough evidence to reject H₀
there is a 30% chance that H₀ is true
questions.explanation: A large p-value means the sample is consistent with H₀, so it is not rejected. That is not proof of H₀, and the p-value is not the probability that either hypothesis is true.

questions.stem: H₀: μ = 500 hours is tested against H₁: μ < 500 hours for a battery. A type II error would be:
options: concluding the mean is less than 500 h when it is 500 h
concluding the mean is less than 500 h when it is less
concluding the mean could be 500 h when it is 500 h
concluding the mean could be 500 h when it is in fact less
questions.explanation: A type II error fails to reject a false H₀: the mean really is below 500 h, but the test does not detect it. Concluding the mean is lower when it is actually 500 h is a type I error.

questions.stem: In terms of conditional probability, the significance level α of a test is:
questions.explanation: α is the probability of a type I error, rejecting H₀ given that it is true. Reversing the condition, Pr(H₀ true | reject H₀), is a different quantity that the test does not control.

questions.stem: For a one-tailed test of H₁: μ > μ₀ at the 5% level, H₀ is rejected when the test statistic z is greater than about:
questions.explanation: Pr(Z > 1.645) ≈ 0.05, so all of the 5% lies in the upper tail. The value 1.96 splits 5% between two tails, for a two-tailed test.

questions.stem: A simulation takes 1000 samples of size 25 from a population with σ = 20. The standard deviation of the 1000 sample means should be close to:
questions.explanation: The standard deviation of the sample mean is σ/√n with n the sample size: 20/√25 = 4. The number of samples simulated does not enter the formula, so 20/√1000 ≈ 0.63 is wrong.

questions.stem: For samples from a normally distributed population, the sample mean is:
options: approximately normal, but only when n ≥ 30
normal only when n is large
normal only when σ is known
exactly normal, for every sample size n
questions.explanation: A linear combination of independent normal variables is normal, and the sample mean is one. The large-sample approximation is needed only when the population is not normal.

questions.stem: Times for two stages of a race are independent, N(30, 4²) and N(45, 3²) minutes. Pr(total time < 80 minutes) is about:
questions.explanation: The total is N(75, 25), with standard deviation 5, so z = (80 − 75)/5 = 1 and Pr(Z < 1) ≈ 0.841. Adding the standard deviations to get 7 gives z ≈ 0.71 and 0.762.

questions.stem: 200 separate 90% confidence intervals for μ are made from independent random samples. About how many will not contain μ?
questions.explanation: Each interval has probability 0.1 of missing μ, so about 0.1 × 200 = 20 miss. About 180 will contain μ, which answers the opposite question.

questions.stem: X₁ and X₂ are independent, each with variance σ². Then Var(X₁ + X₂) and Var(2X₁) are:
questions.explanation: Var(X₁ + X₂) = σ² + σ² = 2σ², but Var(2X₁) = 2²σ² = 4σ². Two independent values partly offset each other, while doubling one value doubles every deviation.

questions.stem: X ~ N(50, 3²) and Y ~ N(40, 4²) are independent. Pr(X > Y) is about:
questions.explanation: X − Y ~ N(10, 25), so Pr(X − Y > 0) = Pr(Z > −2) ≈ 0.977. Using standard deviation 3 + 4 = 7 instead of 5 gives about 0.923.

questions.stem: With σ = 10, what is the smallest sample size for which an approximate 95% confidence interval for μ has a margin of error of at most 2?
questions.explanation: Require 1.96 × 10/√n ≤ 2, so √n ≥ 9.8 and n ≥ 96.04. The sample size must be a whole number at least this, so n = 97; 96 is just too small. A margin of 1 would need 385.

questions.stem: An approximate 95% confidence interval for μ, from a large sample of size 64, is (76.08, 83.92). The sample standard deviation was about:
questions.explanation: The centre is 80 and the margin is 3.92 = 1.96 × s/√64, so s/8 = 2 and s = 16. The value 2 is s/√n, the standard deviation of the sample mean, not of the sample.

questions.stem: With z = 1.8 and a significance level of 0.05, which decision is correct?
options: Reject H₀ for neither of these alternatives
Reject H₀ for H₁: μ ≠ μ₀, but not for H₁: μ > μ₀
Reject H₀ for H₁: μ > μ₀, but not for H₁: μ ≠ μ₀
Reject H₀ for both of these alternatives
questions.explanation: One-tailed, p = Pr(Z > 1.8) ≈ 0.036 < 0.05. Two-tailed, p ≈ 0.072 > 0.05. The same data can be significant in a one-tailed test and not in a two-tailed one.

questions.stem: H₀: μ = 60 is tested against H₁: μ > 60, with σ = 8 and n = 16, at the 5% level. H₀ is rejected when the sample mean is:
questions.explanation: Reject when (sample mean − 60)/(8/√16) > 1.645, that is, when the sample mean exceeds 60 + 1.645 × 2 = 63.29. Using 1.96 gives the two-tailed cut-off, and using σ instead of σ/√n gives 73.16.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for μ is (12.1, 15.3). For a two-tailed test of H₀: μ = 12 at the 5% level, the correct decision is to:
options: reject H₀, since the interval contains the sample mean
not reject H₀, since 12 is below the sample mean
reject H₀, since 12 lies outside the interval
not reject H₀, since 12 is close to the interval
questions.explanation: A two-tailed test at the 5% level rejects H₀ exactly when μ₀ lies outside the 95% confidence interval. The interval always contains the sample mean, so that cannot be a reason to reject.

questions.stem: A can’s mass is N(400, 5²) g and an empty box’s is N(200, 10²) g, independently. A box holding 12 cans has total mass with:
questions.explanation: The total is X₁ + … + X₁₂ + B, with mean 4800 + 200 = 5000 and variance 12 × 25 + 100 = 400, so the standard deviation is 20. Writing 12X for twelve different cans gives 144 × 25 + 100 = 3700.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval has width 8. From the same data, a 90% confidence interval has width about:
questions.explanation: Width is proportional to the quantile, so the new width is 8 × 1.645/1.96 ≈ 6.7. Scaling by 0.90/0.95 gives 7.6, and 9.5 inverts the ratio; a lower confidence level gives a narrower interval.

questions.stem: Twenty independent tests are each carried out at the 5% level, and H₀ is true in every one. The probability of at least one type I error is about:
questions.explanation: Each test avoids a type I error with probability 0.95, so all twenty do with probability 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36, and at least one error has probability 1 − 0.36 ≈ 0.64. Multiplying 20 × 0.05 = 1 double-counts.
